issues.issue: This paragraph makes 11.1 govern vacation "notwithstanding anything contained herein or in University rules, regulations or policies to the contrary," which overrides the incorporation of Staff Handbook fringe benefits in provision 3.2. Whether Handbook vacation payout rights survive depends on reading the two together.

The University's "allotted budget" for football staff "shall not be less than One Million Nine Hundred Thousand Dollars ($1,900,000) per Contract Year," yet the Employee must keep costs "within the University's allotted budget," leaving unclear whether the floor is also the ceiling. The Employee's authority to "establish the salaries of" staff is at the same time made "subject to the prior approval" of the Director of Athletics and "University policy."

Each assistant "may be paid" an extra month's salary on the Employee's recommendation and the Director's approval, so it is unclear whether any entitlement is created at all. The provision fixes deadlines for a payment that no one is bound to make.

The provision lets the University "at any time, with just cause, terminate this Contract or suspend the Employee with or without pay" and thereby be "relieved of all further obligations," but the operative term "just cause" is left to the definition in the following paragraph and to its "normally understood meaning." Whether conduct short of the enumerated grounds supports termination is the central question the words leave open.

The relationship with provision 14.2 is unstated: if a purported just-cause termination is found unjustified, nothing says whether it converts into a unilateral termination without just cause carrying $750,000 per Contract Year in liquidated damages, or leaves the Employee to ordinary breach damages. The two termination routes are drafted as alternatives with no bridge between them.

Ground A requires "conduct by Employee resulting in his conviction of a violation of a criminal statute," yet ground F lets the University terminate for any conduct it "determin[es]" is "seriously prejudicial to the best interests of the University" or that "brings the University into disrepute" or "reflects ... moral turpitude." Whether criminal conduct that produces an arrest or diversion but no conviction is just cause turns on whether the specific ground A limits the general ground F.

"[J]ust cause" is defined to mean the listed grounds "in addition to its normally understood meaning in employment contracts," importing an undefined external standard alongside the enumeration. The definition therefore does not close, and its outer limit must be construed.

The liquidated damages are fixed "in, and only in, the amount of Seven Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($750,000) per Contract Year, pro rated, for the then-unexpired Term," a figure that does not correspond to any compensation component in provisions 3.1, 3.9 or 8.4 and that leaves "pro rated" for the thirteen-month first Contract Year unexplained. What the Employee actually recovers on a no-cause termination is not calculable from the words alone.

The exclusive-remedy language cannot be squared with provision 24.6, which makes "[a]ll remedies, rights, undertakings, obligations and agreements ... cumulative" and preserves every other remedy available at law or in equity. Whether $750,000 per year is the Employee's sole recovery depends on which of the two controls.

Liquidated damages are "paid as if salary, in equal monthly installments in the manner described in provision 3.1," without saying whether the fringe benefits and other salary-linked entitlements of provision 3.2 also continue. The deemed "separation from service" characterization compounds the uncertainty about the payments' nature.

A duty to mitigate, and cessation of payment when other employment begins, cannot readily be squared with provision 14.2's fixed liquidated damages payable "in, and only in, the amount of Seven Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($750,000) per Contract Year." Genuine liquidated damages are not ordinarily reduced by substitute earnings, and the two paragraphs pull in opposite directions.

The offset turns on "the Employee's compensation, from any source (exclusive of the value of standard fringe benefits available to all employees of such employer), in such other employment," a phrase that does not say whether deferred pay, bonuses, buyouts or non-employment income count. "[B]egins any other employment" is likewise undefined as to part-time or unrelated work.

The clawback is triggered whenever the NCAA "after the Employee's termination, finds that there was a violation of NCAA Rules," without any time limit or requirement that the violation relate to his Pitt employment, and it allows the University "to terminate all future payments due hereunder" — payments not confined to provision 14.2. The reach of "all future payments due hereunder" is left open.

The bands are keyed to when notice "is given" or when the resignation "is effective," so a resignation noticed in the fourth Contract Year but effective in the fifth falls literally within both A ($3,000,000) and B ($1,500,000). Nothing in the clause says which figure then applies.

The bar on even "discuss[ing]" prospective employment "directly or indirectly" without "obtaining the consent" of the Director of Athletics states no standard governing consent and no time limit. Whether consent may be withheld arbitrarily, and what counts as an indirect discussion, is left to construction.

The estate receives "his full salary and fringe benefits" through the date of death, but the Contract distinguishes base salary (3.1) from the $150,000 and $350,000 service payments (3.9, 8.4), so whether "full salary" includes those is unclear. Provision 3.2 expressly excludes non-base income from benefit calculations, deepening the ambiguity.

Provision 14.8 terminates the Contract and all University obligations immediately on disability, while provision 14.10 lists 14.8 among the provisions under which University payment obligations expressly continue after termination. The two treatments of the same event cannot both be right.

The exception list preserves obligations "expressly described in provisions 14.2, 14.3, 14.4, 14.7, and 14.8," but 14.8 (disability) and 14.4 (NCAA clawback) describe the extinguishment or recovery of payments rather than any surviving obligation of the University. Reading 14.10 against 14.8 in particular produces a contradiction about what survives.

The restraint applies "within the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania and/or at any other Big East Conference ... member-institution," where "and/or" leaves the geographic reach uncertain, and the one-year period runs "commencing on the date the Employee properly delivers notice," so a resignation without the notice required by 14.5 never starts the clock. Its scope and duration cannot be fixed from the words.

The recited acknowledgment that the covenant "is reasonably limited in duration and geographic scope" sits against the actual scope stated in 14.11 — the entire Commonwealth plus every conference member institution — and against 14.5, which already compensates the University in liquidated damages for the same resignation. The acknowledgment cannot control what the operative words say.

The Contract is said to be "governed by" unspecified "principles and precepts and regulations that relate to equal opportunity employment," a body of norms neither identified nor incorporated. That "governed by" language also sits oddly with the governing-law clause in 22.1.

The Employee must abide by "the non-discrimination and other policies of the University," an open-ended reference to unidentified documents that the University can change at will. Because 14.1G makes breach of University policies just cause, the absence of any identified policy set matters.

The parties must "keep this Contract confidential" and "take whatever measures are necessary" to prevent disclosure, an absolute obligation imposed on a state-related university whose coach's contract is a matter of public interest, and the clause never says what "information contained herein" means. Disclosure may be permitted only through the narrow carve-out in 17.3.

"[P]rivate information" is defined as anything "disclosed to Employee or known by Employee as a consequence of his employment, and not generally known outside the University," a definition with no subject-matter limit and no time limit. It would capture ordinary knowledge of the job as well as genuine confidences.

The perpetual bar on use or disclosure "except as may be absolutely necessary in the performance of his duties for the University" leaves no room for legally compelled disclosure, because the carve-out in 17.3 is expressed to apply only to provision 17.1. Read together, a subpoena would put the Employee in breach of 17.2.

The exception is expressed "[n]otwithstanding anything contained in provision 17.1 to the contrary" and so does not on its face relieve the separate and perpetual confidentiality obligation created by provision 17.2. Whether legally required disclosure is permitted under 17.2 turns on that omission.

Notice to the Employee is given at "his University address or ... his home address last communicated in writing," which fails for the post-termination notices the Contract contemplates under 14.3, 14.4 and 14.11. The clause also does not say when delivery is deemed effective.

The clause binds only "the parties" and says nothing of successors or assigns, which sits uneasily with 14.7's provision for payments to the Employee's estate and with the non-assignment sentence in 24.1. Who else may enforce or be bound is left unstated.

The internal procedure is declared "the exclusive internal dispute resolution mechanism" with a decision "final within the University," while the next paragraph of 20.1 preserves either party's right to go to court. Whether exhaustion of the grievance procedure is a condition precedent to suit cannot be answered from either paragraph alone.

The paragraph is permissive in its first half ("nothing herein shall prevent either party from submitting disputes ... to the proper federal or state court within Allegheny County") and mandatory in its second ("jurisdiction and venue for any such action shall be in a court of appropriate jurisdiction in Allegheny County"). Whether the clause is an exclusive forum selection or merely consent to that forum is ambiguous.

The command that "[a]ll disputes and grievances shall be treated confidentially by both parties, at all times" cannot be squared with the immediately preceding paragraph of 20.1, which authorizes either party to litigate in open federal or state court. One of the two must yield.

This clause makes Pennsylvania law govern, while provision 15.1 separately states that the Contract "shall be governed by" equal-opportunity "principles and precepts and regulations." Two different governing-law statements sit in the same instrument without a priority rule.

The clause says that if a provision is invalid "the Contract shall be ineffective only to the extent of such prohibition," conflating the offending provision with the whole Contract. Whether an invalid liquidated damages or non-compete clause is severed or merely trimmed is left unclear by that mechanical slip.

The requirement that the Contract not be "amended or modified in any manner, except by an instrument in writing signed by both of the parties" cannot be squared with provision 10.1B, under which changes in NCAA, conference or University rules "shall automatically apply to this Contract without the necessity of a written modification." Which of the two governs a rule change is unresolved.

Subparagraph (d), reserving to the University "the right to modify benefits hereunder" with no obligation to "replace or compensate the Employee," cannot easily be squared with the fringe-benefit promise of provision 3.2 or with the specific benefits promised in 3.3 through 3.6. Which benefits are unilaterally modifiable is left open.

The opening sentence excuses performance for "events beyond its reasonable control," but the closing proviso requires that the same events render performance "impossible or unreasonably difficult," two different and inconsistent standards in one paragraph. The illustrative list ("acts of God, war, civil commotion, fire, flood or other casualty and government regulation or restriction") is also expressly non-exhaustive, leaving its outer bound to ejusdem generis.

Making all remedies "cumulative" and preserving every other remedy at law or in equity conflicts with provision 14.2, which entitles the Employee to liquidated damages "in, and only in," a stated amount, and with the liquidated damages in 14.5. Whether the liquidated sums are exclusive or additive turns on which clause controls.

The indemnity extends to sanctions imposed "against the University and/or the Employee," so on its face the Employee must indemnify the University for penalties imposed on himself, and it reaches violations "while he was previously employed at another NCAA member institution." The connector "associated with" any such sanction sets no causal boundary.
